questions.question: Name and locate the three subtropical anticyclones affecting South Africa, and explain why anticyclonic conditions produce clear, dry weather.
questions.expected_answer: The South Atlantic High over the ocean west of the country, the South Indian High over the ocean to the east, and the Kalahari High over the interior plateau. In an anticyclone air subsides, warming adiabatically as it descends, which dissolves cloud; the surface flow diverges outward anticlockwise, and the resulting stability gives clear skies and dry conditions.

questions.question: Explain how the inversion layer's seasonal behaviour produces dry winters and stormy summers over the interior plateau.
questions.expected_answer: In winter the strong Kalahari High creates a low inversion sitting below the escarpment, so moist coastal air cannot climb onto the plateau — the interior is dry, clear and frosty. In summer intense surface heating weakens and lifts the high, the inversion rises above the escarpment, and moist air from the South Indian High flows onto the plateau, feeding the afternoon thunderstorms, including line thunderstorms along the moisture front.

questions.question: Describe the berg wind and the coastal low, and explain the sequence by which a coastal city can be extremely hot in the morning and cool and drizzly by evening on the same winter day.
questions.expected_answer: A berg wind is hot, dry, gusty offshore air that drains off the interior plateau, warming adiabatically at about one degree per hundred metres as it descends more than a kilometre — giving winter heat records and peak fire danger. A coastal low is a shallow low trapped below the escarpment that travels along the coast, usually ahead of a front. Ahead of the low the berg wind blows; behind it cool moist marine air sweeps onshore, dropping temperatures sharply and bringing low cloud and drizzle — hence the morning heat and evening cool change.
